newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poll shows wide indifference among French voters.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows wide indifference among French voters.

text.p: Many French voters are indifferent to next month's parliamentary election, believing neither the ruling centre-right nor opposition Socialists will address their concerns, an opinion poll showed on Tuesday.

The Sofres poll for the daily Le Monde found 38 percent of those surveyed thought a victory by the Socialists would be neither a good thing nor a bad thing. Thirty-six percent thought it would be a good thing and 24 said it would be bad.

The poll found that 35 percent said a centre-right victory in the National Assembly election on May 25 and June 1 would be neither good nor bad while 33 percent said it would be good and 31 percent a bad thing.
The poll questioned 1,000 people aged over 18 on April 25 and 26.
The poll found that voters had slightly greater confidence in the ruling coalition to run France than in the Socialists, but neither party had the confidence of most French people.
Thirty-five percent supported the centre-right, 32 percent the Socialists and 31 percent had confidence in neither.
The poll also found that people did not see much difference in the parties' plans to resolve some of the key issues facing France.

Sixty-one percent of respondents said there would be no difference between the Socialists' and the ruling coalition's ability to stop the rise in unemployment, while 66 percent said the same about ending political funding scandals.

Pluralities said voters reckoned it made no difference whether the government or the Socialists tried to resolve issues such as immigration, putting in place a single European currency and improving their lives.
Only when it came to protecting the generous welfare benefits did a party, in this case the socialists, score.

Sixty-two percent of those polled believed conservative President Jacques Chirac should stay on until his term ends in 2002 even if the Socialists win the snap poll. Thirty-five percent said he should resign and one percent had no opinion.

Another Sofres poll, conducted for Catholic daily La Croix, found that 34 percent of respondents believed the Socialists were best placed to preserve social cohesion, compared to 28 percent who supported the ruling coalition.
Twenty-three percent of respondents said no political party could preserve social cohesion. The newspaper gave no details about the methodology of the poll.
